Positioning for Complex Markets

The Commercial SystemPart 2

By lowob · 7 July 2026 · 9-minute read · Strategy

Positioning is the choice of which buyer you serve, which problem you solve and which alternative you replace. In complex markets that choice has to work without a seller in the room, across a buying group of a dozen people, against a competitor that is usually inaction. Forrester's 2024 study found 13 people involved in the average purchase and 91% of purchases stalling at some point. Research by Matt Dixon and Ted McKenna found 40% to 60% of lost deals end in no decision. A position built for those conditions names the status quo as the alternative, gives each role in the buying group a reason to agree, and carries proof a buyer can check alone.

A complex market, for this piece, is one where the purchase is large relative to the buyer's budget, several functions must agree, the cycle runs for months and the category may still be forming. Most emerging technology sales meet all four conditions. So do many services, infrastructure and regulated products.

Positioning is the first decision in the Strategy part of the commercial system described in Part 1. It shapes what Growth says, which channels Distribution chooses and how Revenue qualifies a deal. We have covered the general distinction between positioning, messaging and branding elsewhere (Positioning vs messaging vs branding). This piece covers what changes when the market is complex.

The position has to work without you in the room

Buyers in complex markets do most of their work alone. Gartner's 2018 survey of 750 B2B buyers in complex purchases found they spent 17% of their buying time meeting potential suppliers, shared across every supplier under consideration. Gartner's 2025 survey of 632 buyers found 61% preferred a rep-free buying experience overall.

Vendor research points the same way. 6sense's 2024 Buyer Experience Report found buyers were nearly 70% through their purchasing process before engaging sellers, and 81% already had a preferred vendor at first contact. These are vendor figures, consistent with Gartner's.

The position is formed before the first meeting, from material the seller did not present: the website, analyst notes, peer conversations, partner recommendations and, increasingly, AI-assisted research. If that material is vague, the buyer fills the gap with the nearest familiar category. Gartner's 2025 survey also found 69% of buyers reported inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers told them. That is a positioning failure that shows up as a sales problem.

The real competitor is usually no decision

Most positioning work defines the competition as other vendors. In complex markets the more common rival is the buyer's current way of working.

Dixon and McKenna's research for The JOLT Effect, which analysed about 2.5 million recorded sales conversations, found 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision, and that some level of buyer indecision was present in roughly nine of ten sales calls. Forrester's 2024 finding that 91% of purchases stall at some point is the same pattern seen from the buyer's side.

Alternative the buyer weighsWhat the position must answerTypical weak answerStronger answer
Do nothingWhy act this quarter rather than next year"Market-leading capability"A cost of delay the buyer can calculate
Build in-houseWhy buy rather than assign the team"Faster time to value"What the internal build would need, in named roles and months
Use an adjacent tool already ownedWhy a new line item"Purpose-built"The specific job the owned tool cannot do, shown
Hire a firm or agencyWhy this model rather than people"Scalable"What the buyer keeps when the engagement ends
A direct competitorWhy us over themFeature comparisonThe buyer type for whom the difference matters most

A position that names a direct competitor as its alternative wins comparisons it is invited to. A position that names the status quo also gets invited. When the category itself is new, the work starts earlier still: our piece on selling into markets without a budget line covers that case (Selling what nobody has a budget line for).

A buying group needs a reason for each role

Forrester's 2024 study, drawing on more than 16,000 global business buyers, found 13 people involved in the average purchase and 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. A position written for the economic buyer alone tends to persuade one person and leave the rest to object.

The fix is not a different message for every role. It is one position that each role can restate in its own terms.

Role in the buying groupWhat they need to believeEvidence that persuades them
Budget holderThe problem costs more than the solution, soonCost of delay, comparable payback
Day-to-day userWork gets easier, not just differentA trial or demonstration on their real task
Technical or security reviewerIt will pass review and not create new riskDocumentation, certifications, architecture
Finance or procurementTerms are standard and the price is defensiblePricing logic, reference contracts
Executive sponsorIt supports a priority they already ownA link to a stated objective

Forrester's 2023 analysis of lead management found that clients who brought three or more buying-group members into the sales process saw a 50% increase in conversion from meeting to closed-won. A position each role can repeat is what makes that possible.

The five components of a position

A position can be written as one sentence: we help a named buyer solve a named problem, instead of their current alternative, because of a difference, and here is the proof. Each component can be tested.

ComponentQuestion it answersWeak versionStrong version
BuyerWho, specifically, and when"Mid-market companies"A segment from the ideal customer profile, with a trigger
ProblemWhat hurts, in the buyer's wordsA capability gapA cost, risk or delay the buyer already measures
AlternativeWhat they would do otherwiseThe nearest vendorThe status quo, named
DifferenceWhat changes if they choose youA feature listOne outcome the alternative cannot produce
ProofWhy they should believe itLogosA checkable result from a buyer like them

The buyer component should come from the ideal customer profile, not from a separate workshop (How to write an ICP). Proof is the component most often missing in emerging technology firms, because there are few customers yet. In that case the honest proof is a design partner's measured result, or a clearly labelled pilot. Our piece on believable case studies sets out what buyers accept (What makes a case study believable).

In a complex market the competitor you most often lose to is the buyer's current way of working.

Testing a position with evidence

A position is a hypothesis about buyers. It can be tested before and after it ships.

Before. Ask five people inside the firm to complete the sentence "we help [who] do [what] instead of [alternative]". If the answers differ, the firm does not yet have a position to test. Then run the same sentence past five recent buyers and five recent losses.

After. Win-loss interviews are the most direct test (What is win-loss analysis?). Three questions do most of the work: what alternative the buyer seriously considered, which role in the buying group raised the hardest objection, and what proof decided it.

McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey found buyers used ten interaction channels on average and more than half would likely switch after a poor cross-channel experience. A useful operational test follows: pick five touchpoints a buyer meets before the first call and check whether each states the same buyer, problem and alternative.

SignalWhat it suggests
Losses mostly to no decisionThe alternative or cost of delay is weak
Losses mostly to one competitorThe difference is unclear for a specific buyer type
Deals stall at security or procurement reviewThe position does not reach those roles
Long first calls spent explaining the categoryThe position is not carrying itself before contact
Wins concentrated in one segmentThe buyer component is too broad

Recording the position as a decision

Positioning is usually treated as a document. In a commercial system it is a decision, and it should be recorded as one: the chosen buyer, problem and alternative, the reason, the owner, the expected effect on win rate or cycle length, and a review date.

That matters for two reasons. First, a recorded position can be graded. If the expected effect does not appear within two or three quarters, the review date forces the question. Second, positions change, and the history matters. When a firm repositions, the old position should be superseded on the record, not deleted, so later analysis can compare deals won under each (Supersede, never overwrite).

This is also where positioning meets The Build Order. A brain that drafts outreach, prepares meeting briefs or answers buyer questions needs the current position as a definition it can read. Without one, each draft improvises its own.

Illustrative example: repositioning against the status quo
Decision
Change the stated alternative from two named competitors to "managing it in spreadsheets and email", and add a cost-of-delay calculation to the first meeting.
Reason and owner
Win-loss interviews showed more than half of recent losses ended with no purchase at all, and buyers rarely mentioned the named competitors. Owned by the commercial lead; reviewed by the founders.
What changed
Website, partner materials and first-call deck were rewritten to the same sentence; the review date was set two quarters out, with no-decision rate as the measure.

Illustrative: a composite of a 45-person emerging technology vendor, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Name the status quo. In complex markets the most common loss is no decision, so the position must explain why to act now.
  • Write for the buying group. One position that each role can restate beats separate messages for each.
  • Ship proof, not adjectives. A checkable result from a similar buyer persuades more than any claim.
  • Record the position. Treat it as a decision with an owner, an expected effect and a review date.
Gateway card

Before you ship a new position

  • The buyer drawn from the ideal customer profile, with a trigger
  • The status quo named as an alternative, with a cost of delay
  • A reason to agree written for each buying-group role
  • One checkable proof point from a buyer like the target
  • Five pre-contact touchpoints checked for the same sentence
  • The position recorded with an owner, expected effect and review date

Common questions

What is positioning in B2B marketing?

Positioning is the decision about which buyer you serve, which problem you solve and which alternative you replace. Messaging and branding follow from it.

How do you position a product in a complex B2B market?

Name the buyer and trigger, treat the status quo as the main alternative, give each role in the buying group a reason to agree, and attach proof a buyer can check without a seller.

Why do so many B2B deals end in no decision?

Buyers face large groups, long cycles and uncertainty about outcomes. Dixon and McKenna's research found 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision, often because buyers feared making the wrong choice.

How often should a company revisit its positioning?

Set a review date when the position is adopted, usually two to four quarters out, and revisit earlier if win-loss evidence shows a consistent new pattern.

  • Forrester, The State of Business Buying, 2024, December 2024. Survey of more than 16,000 buyers; full methodology not public.
  • Challenger, Losing to customer indecision, summarising Dixon and McKenna's research for The JOLT Effect. Commercial training firm's summary of the authors' analysis.
  • Gartner, B2B buyers spend 17% of their time meeting suppliers, August 2018. Survey of 750 buyers; older data.
  • Gartner, 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free buying experience, June 2025. Survey of 632 buyers, fielded August to September 2024.
  • 6sense, 2024 Buyer Experience Report, via Business Wire, October 2024. Vendor research; sample not stated in the release.
  • Forrester, Saying Goodbye to MQLs, November 2023. Analyst blog citing Forrester client data.
  • McKinsey, Five fundamental truths: How B2B winners keep growing, September 2024. Survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers; self-reported.

Next move

Pull your last ten lost deals and mark each as lost to a competitor or lost to no decision. If no decision is the larger group, rewrite the alternative in your position before changing anything else.
